script.title: Why Mary Mallon was locked on an island

lines: A cook lunged at health officials with a long kitchen fork.
Her name was Mary Mallon, and she cooked for rich New York families.
An investigator, George Soper, checked eight families she had cooked for.
Seven of them had caught typhoid fever.
But Mary felt perfectly healthy.
When Soper asked for samples, she grabbed a carving fork.
In 1907, Doctor Sara Josephine Baker came back with the police.
Mary hid in a garden shed.
They found her, and she resisted again.
She was taken away in an ambulance.
Tests found typhoid bacteria in Mary's stool.
She was a healthy carrier: never sick herself, but spreading the disease.
You see, it's like glitter on your hands.
You can't feel it, but everything you touch ends up sparkling.
Officials locked her on North Brother Island.
In 1910, they freed her when she promised never to cook again.
But in 1915, a maternity hospital had twenty-five typhoid cases. Two people died.
The new cook called herself Mary Brown.
Soper matched the handwriting. It was Mary.
Four hundred other healthy carriers were found, but none was confined as long.
Mary stayed on the island for the rest of her life, baking cakes for the patients.

claims.claim: Mallon came at officials with a long kitchen fork when they tried to take her for testing.
Mary Mallon was a cook for wealthy New York families; George Soper found she had worked for eight families, seven of whom suffered typhoid outbreaks.
When Soper asked for samples, Mallon seized a carving fork and he escaped; she believed she was not infected.
On March 20, 1907, Sara Josephine Baker returned with police; Mallon hid in a garden shed, came out fighting and swearing, and Baker sat on her chest in the ambulance.
Her stools showed typhoid bacteria; she was the first person in the U.S. identified as an asymptomatic carrier.
She was quarantined on North Brother Island and released in 1910 after promising not to return to cooking.
In 1915 an outbreak at Sloane Maternity Hospital, where she worked as Mary Brown, had twenty-five cases and two deaths; Soper compared the handwriting.
She was treated differently from four hundred other asymptomatic carriers; none were confined as long.
She remained on the island until her death in 1938, baking cakes she sold to patients and staff.
